newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: NO RULING ON "HOLD MUSIC" COPYRIGHT CASE
The High Court has reserved its judgment in a case which could see Telstra paying copyright for music played down phones while callers wait to speak to someone.
The Australasian Performing Right Association claims Telstra infringes the Copyright Act by offering the service.
APRA says the music on hold service commercially benefits Telstra and its customers and copyright should be paid for material played via CDs and tapes.
APRA's told the Court the industry accepts there are millions of infringements each day where nothing can be done, but when there is a clear cut case of infringement, copyright should be recognised.
RESHUFFLE IN SA CABINET
The new South Australian Cabinet has been sworn in at Government House in Adelaide.
Newcomer Dale Baker will look after finance and mines, while the other new face, Dorothy Kotz, is Minister for Employment, Training and Further Education, Youth Affairs and Correctional Services.
The Premier John Olsen takes on a new portfolio of State Development.
Former Premier Dean Brown will look after Information Technology and Industrial Affairs.
In a surprise, he's also become the state's Aboriginal Affairs minister.
Out of the line-up are Wayne Matthew and Bob Such.
HUSBAND DEFENDS WIFE'S RIGHT TO DIE
The husband of a woman who wants to die under the Northern Territory's voluntary euthanasia law says the views of his wife should be respected by politicians and opponents to the law.
Dave Mills comments follow his wife, Janet's public declaration to want to die because she's suffering from terminal cancer.
Mr Mills says the decision to die is his wife's personal choice and should be respected.
He's called for politicians to stay away from the issue and give the Northern Territory's law a chance to work.
PM KEEN TO REDUCE BLACK DEATHS IN CUSTODY
The Prime Minister admits there's no instant solution to the problem of black deaths in custody.
John Howard has told the new Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission board he's concerned about the incidence of deaths in custody, restating his government's commitment to the problem.
Mr Howard's also assured the new ATSIC board and its chairman, Gatjil Djerrkura, of the Government's goodwill to Aboriginal people and commitment to reconciliation.
He says the Coalition's goals remain more equitable treatment of indigenous people, redressing disadvantage and addressing the continuing high levels of deaths in custody.
AMP POISED FOR LISTING ON STOCK EXCHANGE
The third of Australia's big insurers, the AMP Society has announced plans to list on the stock exchange.
This follows the successful list of National Mutual in October, and plans for Colonial Mutual shares to be on the board early next year.
The AMP Society will de-mutualize which involves policy holders giving up their membership rights in exchange for shares in the new company.
Policy holders will be asked to vote on the proposal late next year, with the hope of listing on the Australian and New Zealand Stock Exchanges in late 1998.
The company will also consider listing in the United Kingdom.
MINISTER DEFENDS JETSETTING TRIP
Arts Minister Richard Alston has defended an international tour of art galleries planned for next month, saying it's vital to his portfolio to have a comprehensive world view of culture.
Senator Alston has come under Opposition criticism over a trip that will take him to London, New York, Los Angeles and Hawaii.
He says it's in the taxpayer's interest that he visits overseas art galleries to upgrade his cultural knowledge, but the ALP claims the trip is a waste of public money.
DEFENCE FORCE SEX COMPLAINT DROPPED
One of three women who made complaints about sexual assault at the Australian Defence Force Academy has withdrawn the complaint.
The three cadets had made separate complaints about the incidents, two of which are alleged to have occurred on campus and one off campus.
The attacks are alleged to have taken place in the past 12 months and are being investigated by the Australian Federal Police.
But the AFP says the complaint about the off campus assault has now been withdrawn.
MINTS JOIN FORCES FOR SYDNEY OLYMPICS
Federal Treasurer Peter Costello has announced the Royal Australian Mint and the Perth Mint have signed a memorandum of understanding to undertake the Sydney 2000 Olympic Coin program.
The memorandum has been signed with the Sydney Organising Commmittee for the Games.
The Treasurer says it's the first time the two mints have joined forces for an international coin programme.
Mr Costello says the program will be launched in September next year and cover a four year period leading up to 2000.
- - - -, UNION SAYS JOBS NEEDN'T BE CUT
The union covering Victorian public servants says an Industrial Relations Commission decision should not lead to any job losses.
The IRC has granted back-pay and benefits estimated at up to 50 million dollars to about 23,000 Victorian public servants.
This has prompted Premier Jeff Kennett to foreshadow job cuts to fudn the payouts.
But the Community and Public Sector Union's Karen Batt says there is already enough money in the State's budget to allow the pay rises, without cutting jobs.
BY-ELECTION FOR FRASER ON 1ST FEBRUARY
House of Representatives Speaker, Bob Halverson, has announced the by-election for the Federal seat of Fraser, in Canberra, will be on Saturday February first next year.
The by-election's been caused by the resignation of the sitting Labor member, John Langmore.
The electoral roll will close on Monday the sixth of January, and nominations will close on friday the tenth of January.
